newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKETS OUTLOOK - Prodding new support.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKETS OUTLOOK - Prodding new support.

text.p: U.S. credit markets should see Treasury yields prod the rich side of the range on Wednesday barring major a surprise change to the congressional make-up from Tuesday's election, analysts said.

The only event that could pose a hurdle outside of election upsets is Wednesday's auction of $10.0 billion 10-year notes, analysts said. However, some noted the "okay" three-year auction on Tuesday and a fearless attitude ahead of Wednesday's 10-year sale suggests government yields may push lower yet.
"Barring any takeover of the house the market will probably have a reasonably good tone," said Cary Leahey, senior vice president and economist at Lehman Brothers.

In the event of a Democratic surge in the house, Norwest Corp Economist Larry Wipf said a short-term sell-off in both stocks and bonds would ensue. More likley, however, Wipf said lackluster reaction will leave the markets to focus elsewhere.
"Assuming the status quo --- (President Bill) Clinton gets reelected and a Republican controlled congress is maintained -- you won't get that much reaction in the financial markets due to politics."
Leahey said the muted reaction would take place under a favorable umbrella, however, with little on the horizon to drain market sentiments.
"It's another dataless day, we're unlikely to have any tape bombs from the Fed given the outstanding FBI probe so I don't think much is going to get in the way of the markets," Leahey said.

The second leg of the Treasury's refunding may prompt some concession, but the degree will probably be minimal based on strong buying for the Treasury curve on Tuesday, said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at CS First Boston Corp.
"Given the scope of interest that we saw throughout the day it's very possible that people are short and need to buy them in the auction," Alexy said.
The 10-year T-note gained more than 1/2 point on Tuesday to yield 6.27 percent.

Tuesday's sale of $18.5 billion in three-year notes came in mostly as expected at an average yield of 5.879 percent, dealers said. Economists said non-competitive bids were a lower than expected $564 million, however.

Strong overnight buying with the help of bond-friendly economic data have pushed Treasury yields toward the bottom of the range, where they are likely to hover until the delivery of producer and consumer price data next week, analysts said.

Leahey said the next level of support for the benchmark 30-year bond is around 6.58 percent, only one basis point lower than Tuesday's closing yield of 6.59 percent after a one point rally. Should the bond break through, its yield may gravitate as low as 6.33 percent, he added.
"I think (current levels) are about as good as you can get for now," he said.

"You need (November) the 13th with maybe a great (Producer Price Index) to get there." Away from the elections, Alexy said another spate of overnight buying like that seen on Monday night could push Treasuries higher.

"Last night almost everything else in the world rallied," Alexy said. "There was almost a basis point rally in the middle of the German curve, Canada did a couple of basis points so that has to be watched pretty closely because the markets are moving together increasingly so."
The Fed Funds rate is expected to open on Wednesday between 5-3/8 percent and 5-1/2 percent. -- 212-859-1672
